How to Prepare Print-Ready Files for Direct Mail

In This Article

  • The Four Non-Negotiable Specs
  • Font Handling: Outlined or Embedded
  • File Formats We Accept
  • What Happens When We Receive Your File
  • Common File Errors and How to Fix Them
  • Files From Canva, Word, and Other Non-Professional Tools

The difference between a file that goes to press smoothly and one that causes a delay — or worse, a reprint — comes down to a handful of specifications that most designers learn from making mistakes. This guide is the shortcut.

Whether you’re a business owner working in Canva, a designer in InDesign, or a marketing coordinator submitting files to us at Cornerstone Services in New Paltz for the first time, here are the exact settings your print file needs.

The Four Non-Negotiable Specs

1. Color Mode: CMYK, Not RGB

Your computer screen displays color in RGB — a combination of red, green, and blue light. Printers use CMYK — cyan, magenta, yellow, and black inks. The two systems produce different color ranges.

The problem: vivid screen colors often don’t exist in CMYK. A saturated blue on a screen might print as a noticeably different shade in CMYK. If you build your design in RGB and submit it, the printer’s system will convert it to CMYK automatically — but that conversion may shift colors in ways you didn’t expect and won’t catch until you see the printed piece.

The fix: Work in CMYK from the start. In Adobe InDesign or Illustrator, set your document color mode to CMYK when you create the file. In Photoshop, open images and convert to CMYK (Image > Mode > CMYK Color) before placing them. In Canva, the “Print” export option converts to CMYK, but not all design elements translate perfectly.

2. Resolution: 300 DPI at Print Size

DPI stands for dots per inch — the density of pixel information in an image. Screen images are typically 72 DPI. Print requires 300 DPI. At 72 DPI, a printed image looks blurry and pixelated.

The rule: every photo or image placed in your print file must be at least 300 DPI at the size it will print. If a photo is 300 DPI at 4 inches wide and you enlarge it to 8 inches wide in your design software, it becomes 150 DPI — not enough for print.

Check resolution in Photoshop: Image menu > Image Size. The resolution field shows DPI at the current print dimensions. If it’s under 300, either source a higher-resolution version of the image or reduce the print size.

3. Bleed: 0.125 Inch on All Sides

Bleed is the extension of your background color or design beyond the intended trim edge. Commercial printers cut printed sheets to finished size using an industrial paper cutter. The cutter does not land in exactly the same position on every cut — there is a small tolerance of 1/16 inch or less.

If your background color or photo ends exactly at the trim edge and the cutter moves 1/16 inch inward, a thin white gap appears at the edge of the piece. Bleed eliminates this by extending the design 1/8 inch beyond the trim — if the cutter moves in any direction within its tolerance, the design still covers the full face.

How to set it up: Build your document at the finished size (e.g., 6 x 9 inches for a 6x9 postcard) plus 0.125 inch on each side (6.25 x 9.25 inches). Extend any backgrounds, photos, or design elements to the outer edge of this larger document. The printer’s press PDF will include bleed marks showing where the trim will occur.

Designs with a white background that does not extend to the edge (a border design, for example) do not require bleed — there is no color to bleed.

4. Safe Zone: 0.125–0.25 Inch Inside the Trim

The inverse of bleed: just as you extend backgrounds beyond the trim, you keep critical content away from the trim edge. The 0.125 inch (1/8 inch) safe zone is the minimum — content placed closer to the trim edge risks being cropped in production.

For anything critical — your phone number, logo, CTA, a headline — stay at least 0.25 inch (1/4 inch) inside the trim edge. This gives the cutter’s tolerance a margin on both sides.

Font Handling: Outlined or Embedded

Fonts are software. If a PDF references a font that is not installed on the printer’s system and is not embedded in the PDF, the printer’s system substitutes a default font — usually something generic like Helvetica — replacing your typography.

Solution 1: Outline your fonts. In Illustrator, select all text and go to Type > Create Outlines. This converts the text from live, editable characters into vector shapes — no longer dependent on the font software being installed. The shapes cannot be edited as text afterward, so save an outlined version separately from your working file.

Solution 2: Export as PDF/X-1a or PDF/X-4. These PDF standards embed all fonts in the file automatically. InDesign’s built-in PDF export presets handle this. For Illustrator and Photoshop, using the “Save As > Adobe PDF” option with the PDF/X-1a preset embeds fonts and flattens transparency.

File Formats We Accept

FormatNotes
PDF (preferred)PDF/X-1a or PDF/X-4 for best compatibility
InDesign packageInclude all linked files and fonts
Illustrator AI/EPSFonts must be outlined
Photoshop PSDCMYK, 300 DPI, layers flattened or organized
Canva “Print” PDFUse the PDF Print export option (not PDF Screen)

What we do not accept: Word documents, PowerPoint files, or web image exports (JPG at 72 DPI). These require rebuilding the design at print resolution before production.

What Happens When We Receive Your File

At Cornerstone, every submitted file goes through a preflight review before it goes to press. We check:

  • Document dimensions and bleed setup
  • Color mode (CMYK confirmed, RGB flagged)
  • Image resolution at placed sizes
  • Font embedding or outline status
  • Transparency flattening
  • USPS compliance for direct mail pieces (size, clear zones, indicia placement)

If we find issues, we contact you before production — not after. Most common file issues take 30–60 minutes to resolve. The ones that require going back to your designer take longer, which is why we’d rather catch them on day one than day five.

Common File Errors and How to Fix Them

These are the five most frequent issues we catch during preflight at Cornerstone — and how to prevent them:

1. Low-resolution images scaled up in the layout. A photo pulled from a website (typically 72 DPI, 600 pixels wide) placed in a design at 6 inches wide prints at roughly 100 DPI — visibly blurry. The fix: source the original photo from the photographer or use a stock image purchased at high resolution. If the original file is unavailable, reduce the image’s placement size in the layout until the effective DPI reaches 300 or higher.

2. Spot colors mixed with CMYK. Some designs include Pantone spot colors alongside CMYK process colors. Spot colors are used for exact color matching (brand identity work, logo colors) and require a dedicated ink channel on press. If your job is printing as a standard 4-color (CMYK) process job, convert all spot colors to their CMYK equivalents in your design software before exporting. Leaving spot colors in a CMYK-intended file can produce unexpected color output.

3. Transparency not flattened. Drop shadows, gradient fills, and opacity effects in Illustrator and InDesign use transparency. PDF/X-1a export flattens transparency automatically. If you export a standard PDF without flattening, certain elements may not render correctly on press — drop shadows may disappear, gradient edges may show banding, or overlapping transparent elements may produce unexpected color blending. Use PDF/X-1a or PDF/X-4 export presets to avoid this.

4. Text too close to the fold or trim. On folded pieces (brochures, self-mailers), the fold line has the same tolerance issue as the trim edge. Text that runs right up to the fold may appear misaligned when the piece is folded — one word on the left panel, the rest on the right. Keep text at least 0.25 inch from any fold line.

5. Black text built in CMYK instead of 100% K. Small body text should be set as 100% black (K only) — not a rich black built from all four CMYK channels (e.g., C:60 M:40 Y:40 K:100). Rich black on body text creates registration issues on press — if the four ink channels are even slightly misaligned, the text shows color fringing (a colored halo around each letter). Use rich black only for large headlines and graphic elements where the coverage area justifies the additional ink channels.

Files From Canva, Word, and Other Non-Professional Tools

We receive files from every design platform, including consumer tools. Here’s how to get the best results from each:

Canva: Use the “PDF Print” export option — not “PDF Standard.” The Print export embeds fonts, converts to CMYK (approximately), and includes crop marks. Canva files often have resolution issues with free stock images — Canva Pro images are typically 300 DPI, but free images may be lower. We check resolution during preflight.

Microsoft Word and PowerPoint: These are not print design tools, but we work with files from them when that’s what a client has. The biggest issues: low-resolution images, RGB color mode, and fonts that don’t embed in PDF export. If you must use Word or PowerPoint, export as PDF with the “Best for printing” option selected. We will likely need to adjust the file for press — factor in 30–60 minutes of file prep time.

Google Docs/Slides: Similar issues to Word/PowerPoint, with the added challenge that Google’s PDF export does not embed all fonts reliably. If using Google tools, convert text to a common system font (Arial, Times New Roman) before exporting, or accept that the printer may need to substitute fonts.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a print-ready file?

A print-ready file is a digital document set up to the exact specifications a commercial printer needs to produce the piece without corrections or modifications. For most direct mail printing jobs, a print-ready PDF is the standard deliverable — built at the correct finished size plus bleed, with all fonts embedded or outlined, images at 300 DPI minimum, and colors set to CMYK. A properly prepared print-ready file goes directly to press without requiring changes.

What is bleed and why does it matter for printing?

Bleed is the extension of your background color, photo, or design element beyond the finished trim edge of the piece. Commercial printers cut printed sheets to the finished size using an industrial cutter, and the cut is never perfectly on the same line as the digital edge. A 0.125 inch (1/8 inch) bleed on all sides ensures that if the cutter cuts 1/16 of an inch off the expected line in either direction, no white gap appears at the edge of the piece. Any design that extends to the trim edge must have bleed set up; designs with a white background or border do not require bleed.

What resolution do images need to be for printing?

Images used in print files must be 300 DPI (dots per inch) at the size they will be printed. An image that looks sharp on a computer screen at 72 DPI will print blurry and pixelated. Smartphone photos are often adequate resolution — most modern smartphone cameras produce files that are sufficient for print at small to medium sizes. The problem is resizing: if you take a 72 DPI web image and enlarge it in your design software, the resolution does not increase — it gets worse. Always source high-resolution photos or request them from your photographer.

What is the difference between RGB and CMYK color?

RGB (Red, Green, Blue) is the color mode used by computer screens and digital cameras. CMYK (Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Black) is the color mode used by printing presses. They produce different color ranges — some vivid screen colors cannot be reproduced in CMYK printing, and the conversion from RGB to CMYK shifts colors. Always set up print files in CMYK from the start. Files submitted in RGB will be converted automatically, and some colors will shift in ways that may not match your brand standards.
